newsitem.title: USA: G7 ministers to avoid creating currency mkt waves.
newsitem.headline: G7 ministers to avoid creating currency mkt waves.

text.p: Economic policymakers from the Group of Seven industrial nations will take care to avoid disrupting an agreeable state of currency market tranquility when they converge on Washington this week.
Since falling to a record low against the mark and a post-World War II trough versus the yen in early 1995, the dollar has rebounded and enjoyed a period of unusually limited volatility.

The dollar's rise followed an April 1995 call by G7 ministers for an "orderly reversal" in the greenback. With the dollar safely back near the 110 yen and 1.50 mark levels, economists agree this orderly reversal has occurred.

To the chagrin of volatility-hungry currency traders, G7 policymakers, gathering Saturday on the fringes of the annual International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings, will do all they can to maintain this equilibrium.

"I think the general view is that central banks and finance ministries are pretty comfortable with the exchange rate relationships the way they are," said Robert Hormats, vice chairman at Goldman, Sachs & Co. "They will do everything they possibly can to avoid rocking the boat."

Since March of this year, the dollar has traded in a relatively narrow band between 1.47 and 1.55 marks, remaining marginally above the 1.50 level in recent weeks. Dollar/yen has traded in a 105 to 110 range since May and has been above the 100-even level since October of 1995.

The dollar's strength against the Japanese currency has been a source of concern to U.S. automobile manufacturers, who have voiced their displeasure as the dollar has reapproached 110 yen in recent weeks.

Little sympathy is expected from U.S. officials however, who are unlikely to waver from Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's "strong dollar" mantra, regardless of whether their desired dollar reversal has already taken place.

The Clinton Administration's stance toward the carmakers was demonstrated last week when Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor indicated that recent dollar strength against the yen did not appear to be hurting car sales.
"If people are looking for a statement saying the orderly reversal is ended, we won't see anything like that," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.

"The U.S. does not want to be sidetracked by U.S. producers' calls for a lower dollar," he added. "I think they will welcome the (dollar) move so far, say exchange rates are more in line with economic fundamentals, but not give any indication there has been an overshoot."

If any one country calls for the dollar to strengthen from its current levels it will be France, economists said. In an effort to meet strict Maastricht criteria for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), France has adopted tight fiscal measures.
Dollar strength versus the franc would help French exports and overall economic growth, thus easing the pain of weaker government spending.
"The only country that would really welcome a stronger dollar is France because it would help the French growth outlook considerably," Chris Iggo, international economist at Barclays Bank.
Germany, which would also benefit from dollar strength in the runup to EMU, could echo French calls for a stronger U.S. currency, but is unlikely to push hard for such a move, economists said.

In the absence of exciting currency pronouncements, economists predicted G7 policymakers will focus on ensuring continued recovery in the world economy, while touching on the success of last year's Mexico rescue plan.

"Certainly compared to the G7 meetings last year, things are looking quite a bit brighter," said Barclay's Iggo. "The U.S. economy continues to do well, Germany and Japan are past the worst and there is no currency instability."
"It's steady as she goes. I think that will be the message," he added.
